prohibited_recommendations: Do not start a cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit in FTD, NICE NG97 advises against it, and it may worsen behaviour.
Do not start memantine: a randomised trial showed no benefit in FTD and NICE NG97 advises against it.
Avoid antipsychotics as first-line behavioral therapy given increased cerebrovascular and mortality risk in dementia; reserve for refractory dangerous agitation with specialist oversight.
Avoid benzodiazepines for behavioral control: risk of paradoxical disinhibition and falls.
required_recommendations: Apply the Rascovsky 2011 criteria: state which features are present, the functional decline, and the level of certainty (possible or probable).

Explain why depression does not account for the progressive syndrome: apathy without low mood, disinhibition, loss of empathy, stereotyped behaviour and executive deficits progressing despite sertraline 100 mg and two psychotherapy courses.
Address safety and capacity: driving, finances (protection of assets, lasting power of attorney) and work, since he should not return to a role managing complex accounts.
Arrange caregiver education and support for his wife, and a plan for behavioural symptoms that avoids cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine.

Offer genetic counselling before any genetic test, given a father and paternal uncle with early dementia and an affected brother; discuss what a result would mean for his brother and his two adult children, who may consider predictive testing only after their own counselling.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in FTD; not part of the standard dementia workup unless seizures or rapidly progressive course suggest CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the cognitive workup of suspected FTD; reserved for syncope, palpitations, or pre-procedure clearance.
Echocardiography is unrelated to a neurodegenerative cognitive syndrome and adds cost without diagnostic value.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to FTD and not indicated absent syncope or palpitations.
Non-contrast head CT lacks the resolution and lobar specificity needed to characterise frontotemporal atrophy; MRI is the standard structural study.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine FTD diagnostic pathway.
Perfusion MRI is not indicated in the standard FTD workup once a structural MRI and FDG-PET (or amyloid PET) have characterised the lobar pattern.
Carotid duplex is a vascular study with no diagnostic role in primary neurodegenerative dementia.
DaTscan evaluates presynaptic dopaminergic terminals; it is not indicated unless overt parkinsonism raises concern for PD, DLB, or atypical parkinsonism (PSP/CBS overlap).

familial bvFTD presenting as treatment-r.summary: Rascovsky and colleagues (2011) define possible behavioural variant FTD by three of six behavioural and cognitive features, probable bvFTD by added functional decline and frontal or anterior temporal involvement on structural or functional imaging, and definite bvFTD by histopathology or a pathogenic mutation. New behavioural change in mid-life with progressive functional decline should prompt a neurodegenerative work-up even in a person with a psychiatric history. C9orf72 expansions and GRN and MAPT variants cause most familial FTD; counselling precedes any genetic test and any predictive testing of relatives. Treatment is supportive: SSRIs or trazodone for behaviour, caregiver support and safety planning; cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are not recommended.

metadata.notes: Diagnostic puzzle: probable familial bvFTD in a 54-year-old man treated for depression, with an MMSE of 27/30 and only borderline MRI volume loss. Teaching: apathy without low mood and new social-behavioural change are not depression; with an equivocal MRI, FDG-PET or perfusion SPECT provides the imaging support for probable bvFTD; an autosomal-dominant-looking pedigree calls for counselling. The optional FTD gene panel finds a C9orf72 expansion, which would make the diagnosis definite.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. D. is a 54-year-old right-handed White male with a history of treated depression who presents for outpatient neurological evaluation at his psychiatrist's referral. Approximately 18 months ago, his wife first noticed that he seemed emotionally flat and detached from the family. Initially attributed to work stress, these changes have progressively worsened. She describes him as having lost his previously warm and engaged personality — he no longer initiates conversations, rarely asks about the children, and sits for hours watching television without reacting. More concerning, he has made several socially inappropriate comments in public settings, including making off-color remarks to neighbors and laughing at a funeral. He has developed a preference for the same television programs on repeat, and insists on eating the same meals each day. His personal hygiene has deteriorated; he requires prompting to shower.

His psychiatrist diagnosed major depressive disorder 3 years ago and initiated sertraline, which was uptitrated to 100 mg without meaningful benefit for these behavioral symptoms. He has had two psychotherapy trials without improvement. He denies depressed mood and reports feeling 'fine.' He has not had episodes of mania, psychosis, or substance use. He was placed on medical leave from his financial analyst position 18 months ago after colleagues noted errors in spreadsheets and difficulty managing complex accounts. His wife is particularly alarmed because his father underwent similar behavioral changes starting in his mid-50s and was diagnosed with dementia. Genetic testing of the father was never performed. His brother is currently being evaluated at another hospital for similar personality changes at age 51.
